subtype: Approach: buffer and slack planning for late payments [Thinking]
passage:
Vidya, people ask why my agency survived year one when two of my friends' didn't. Honestly? I'm Eshaan, and I'm a pessimist about invoices. Before I spent a rupee, I asked myself: when do clients here actually pay? Not what the contract says. What really happens. My old boss used to wait sixty, sometimes ninety days. So I built my plan as if every invoice arrives a full quarter after the due date. If a client promises April, my sheet says July.
Then, on top of that, I kept two months of costs in a separate account that I don't touch. Not for growth, not for a new laptop. Pure reserve.
In month five, our biggest client paid eighty-three days late. My friends would have missed salaries. We just waited. It was boring, Vidya. Boring is exactly what I wanted.

qa.a: Eighty-three days late.

qa.a: Eshaan felt calm, even relieved, when the late payment came, because the plan had expected it; the lack of panic was the goal.

qa.q: What else could strengthen Eshaan's plan?
qa.a: Eshaan could agree clear payment terms and polite reminder dates with clients, while still keeping the reserve.

qa.q: How might the agency's staff have experienced the late payment?

I was copying the meal-kit startup across town. They had a smart desk, a full-time designer and ads everywhere. So I got the desk, hired a designer and started ads too. What I didn't think about is that they had raised roughly ten times what I had saved.
By May my money was nearly gone. I had forty customers and a beautiful brand. I had also stopped sleeping properly and snapped at my designer, who didn't deserve it.
I've given up the desk and paused the ads. I'd like to come and talk about what a plan my size looks like. Is next week possible?
Pema

Tejas and I share a flat in Pune and a startup, so I saw the whole thing up close. In March our company account had seven months left. Tejas came home one night and said, "I've taken two consulting contracts. Mornings only, backend work for a logistics firm and a school."
I was annoyed at first; I thought he was losing faith in our product. But he had done the maths on the fridge whiteboard. If his rent and food came from consulting, the company money only had to pay for servers and my stipend. He crossed out "seven months" and wrote "twelve".
From then on he consulted till noon, ate lunch standing up and switched to our app. He looked tired some weeks. But in September, when other founders we knew were shutting down, we still had money in the bank.
— Uday

Before either of them moved a rupee from savings, Afreen made Charu sit on the floor of her Bandra flat with a pad of sticky notes.
"It's March next year. Our company is dead. Why?"
Charu laughed, then didn't. "Nobody found us. We built it and no salon knew it existed."
Afreen wrote: No way to reach customers. "What else?"
"One of us left. Maybe me, if my father's shop needs me."
"And?"
"Salons took six months to decide, and we ran out before they paid."
Three yellow notes on the wall. Afreen said, "Okay. One small check for each, this month." They agreed: get ten salons to a free demo through one beauty-supply distributor; talk honestly about the shop on Sunday; and ask three salon owners how long they usually take to buy software.
Only then did they open their banking apps.

qa.q: What three reasons did they write on the wall?
qa.a: No way to reach customers, one of them leaving, and salons taking six months to decide.

qa.q: What made Charu stop laughing?
qa.a: Charu saw the exercise was serious and felt uneasy facing real risks, like possibly having to leave for the father's shop.

qa.q: Which early check seems most urgent, and why?
qa.a: Asking salon owners how long they take to buy, because a slow sale could drain their savings before any payment arrives.

qa.a: If the shop needs Charu, the team could lose a partner, which is why they agreed to talk about it honestly on Sunday.

"It's fine, Vandana. The company's been closed a year. Ask."

Our study-planner app had a leak we couldn't plug: most students deleted it within six days. Anjali and I had redesigned the first screens three times. Nothing moved.
One night Anjali said, "Lokesh, let's just keep asking why." So we did, on the whiteboard.
Why do they leave? They stop opening it after day two.
Why? The reminders feel like nagging.
Why does it feel like nagging? They didn't choose it; their parents installed it.
Why did the parents install it? The school told them to.
Why does that matter? Because the students were never the ones deciding. Parents and teachers were.
I remember staring at that last line. We had been designing for teenagers who never wanted the app. We needed to talk to the people who actually chose it and paid for it.

January, year three. Yusuf and Aparna's accounting app has 400 users, the same as last June. Aparna suggests pausing to ask why. Yusuf shakes his head. "Two years, Aparna. We can't just stop. Let's add invoicing."
April. Invoicing ships after eleven weeks and two freelancers. Users: 410. Yusuf says, "It's the reports. Nobody has proper reports." They start on reports. The savings drop below six months.
August. Reports ship. Then a dark theme. Then a tax calculator. The app now has twenty-three features. Users: 405. Aparna sits on the office stairs with the spreadsheet. "Every release costs more, and nothing moves." Yusuf is quiet. Then he says, "If we stop now, those two years were for nothing."
Aparna says softly, "They're spent either way."

qa.a: Yusuf felt that stopping would mean the two years were wasted, and dread of admitting that kept him building.

I sit next to the product team at our salon-software startup, so I watched Gurpreet the week the numbers came in. The dashboard showed that almost every salon used one thing: the reminder message sent to customers the day before an appointment. Stock tracking, staff rota, loyalty points: barely touched.
Gurpreet printed the chart and taped it to the wall. For two days I saw Gurpreet standing in front of it, arms folded, saying things aloud like, "They pay for the reminder. The rest is what we thought they wanted." On Thursday, in the team meeting, Gurpreet said, "I think the reminder is the product. Everything else is decoration." The designer who built loyalty points looked hurt.
I can't say whether it was easy for Gurpreet to say. But by Friday the roadmap on the whiteboard had one word circled: reminders.
— Harsha
